final_proof:
Let \(K\) be a subfield of \(\mathbb C\). Its multiplicative identity is the same as that of \(\mathbb C\): indeed, if \(1_K\) denotes the identity of \(K\), choose \(a\in K\) with \(a\ne 0\). Then, with all operations viewed in \(\mathbb C\), we have \(1_Ka=a=1_{\mathbb C}a\); multiplying by \(a^{-1}\in K\subseteq\mathbb C\) gives \(1_K=1_{\mathbb C}\). (Equivalently, this equality is part of the usual definition of subfield.)

Recall that the characteristic of a field is the least positive integer \(n\), if one exists, for which \(n\cdot 1=0\), and is \(0\) if no such positive integer exists. For every positive integer \(n\),
\[
n\cdot 1_K=n\cdot 1_{\mathbb C}=\underbrace{1_{\mathbb C}+\cdots+1_{\mathbb C}}_{n\text{ summands}}=n+0i.
\]
This complex number is nonzero, since its modulus is \(n>0\). Thus there is no positive integer \(n\) such that \(n\cdot 1_K=0\). By the definition of characteristic, \(\operatorname{char}(K)=0\). Since \(K\) was arbitrary, every subfield of \(\mathbb C\) has characteristic \(0\).
